Paragraph: Bharadvaja requested Bharata to stay on at his hermitage one more day, so as to offer him the full honors due to a noble guest.Disregarding Bharata's protests, the sage even asked the armies into the hermitage. Bharata said that kings or princes should always spare hermitages from desecration, as spirited horses and intoxicated elephants could damage plants and cottages." But the sage insisted. Invoking Visvakarma to offer the best to his guests he said, "May Viswakarma, the architect of the world, create shelter to house and entertain my guests. May Indra, Varuna, Yama and Kubera provide food and may the rivers be diverted here bringing with them the best of wines. I invite Rambha, Menaka and Urvasi along with Thumbura. May they hasten here along with their musical instruments and may the moon provide us with sumptuous food!" Thus invoked the emaciated sage, who could survive on nothing more than sheer yogic power, without partaking of any food, if need be.He stood facing east, with joined palms, in an attitude of worship and welcomed those whom he had invoked. Celestial clouds showered flowers, to the reverberating sound of divine drums and gongs, while the earth and sky hummed a melody. Then there appeared a veritable paradise. Created by the Devas and invoked by Bharadvaja, its unparalleled beauty upon earth rivaled with the very heavens.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Bharadvaja insists on extending lavish hospitality to Bharata and his entire army, despite Bharata's protests about desecrating the hermitage. The challenge is Bharadvaja's determination to fulfill his duty as a host through supernatural means, overriding practical concerns.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Bharadvaja demonstrates an unwavering commitment to the Vedic principle of Athithi Devo Bhava (Guest is God), ensuring the 'full honors due to a noble guest'. He uses his ascetic and yogic powers to supernaturally manifest a paradise, showing the power of spiritual realization over material limitations. Bharata's protest, though disregarded, highlights a respect for the sanctity of hermitages.
Outcome/Resolution: Bharadvaja successfully invokes celestial beings and divine powers, transforming his hermitage into a 'veritable paradise' to host Bharata and his army. This magical creation resolves the immediate need for shelter and provisions, showcasing the sage's immense spiritual prowess and his commitment to hospitality.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Athithi Devo Bhava (Guest is God: Bharadvaja's paramount duty to offer full honors to his guests, even beyond conventional means.)
Tapasya (Austerity/Yogic Power: Bharadvaja's ability to invoke celestial beings and create a paradise through 'sheer yogic power' is a direct result of his Tapasya.)
Sankalpa Shakti (Power of intention/Will: The sage's firm intention and invocation manifest a supernatural reality, demonstrating the power of spiritual resolve.)
Anugraha (Divine Grace/Blessing: The showering of flowers and the humming melody suggest a divine blessing accompanying the manifestation of paradise.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage exemplifies the profound spiritual concept of Athithi Devo Bhava (Guest is God) through Bharadvaja's unwavering commitment to hospitality, even beyond the material realm. His extraordinary ability to manifest a 'veritable paradise' through 'sheer yogic power' showcases the immense results of Tapasya (austerity) and the potent Sankalpa Shakti (power of intention), culminating in an experience of Anugraha (divine grace).
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharadvaja's insistence on hosting, despite Bharata's initial protests, highlights a strong sense of purpose and a mastery of his own will, allowing him to manage stress by focusing on his duty of hospitality. Bharata's concerns about desecration reflect a psychological sensitivity to environmental impact, though ultimately overridden by the sage's conviction. The creation of paradise serves as a profound psychological relief for the weary travelers, indicating a successful stress management outcome through a benevolent, almost magical, provision of comfort.
